content: 1. During antenatal care (ANC), the proportion of new antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiations occurring during pregnancy, rather than at delivery, can be calculated by dividing the number of cases in category 2 by the sum of cases in categories 2 and 3. 2. ART coverage in pregnant women is a critical indicator for monitoring the percentage of HIV-exposed breastfeeding infants whose mothers are receiving ART at 12 and 24 months postpartum. This indicator evaluates the program's ability to reduce the risk of HIV transmission through breastfeeding, which is a key component of the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) strategy. 3. In many countries, the average breastfeeding period is 18–24 months, representing a significant risk period for HIV-exposed infants. Retaining HIV-positive mothers on ART during this period is essential to maintaining maternal health and preventing infant infection. 4. The percentage of HIV-exposed infants with a known final HIV outcome status measures the quality of program follow-up to track exposed infants and determine their final HIV status. Effective PMTCT programs must follow HIV-exposed infants through the breastfeeding period to ensure comprehensive service delivery and support for both mothers and infants. 5. The percentage of pregnant women who are HIV-positive at the time of their first test during the current pregnancy measures HIV prevalence among ANC attendees. This includes women diagnosed with HIV before their first ANC visit and those testing positive during their current pregnancy. 6. HIV prevalence among ANC attendees is used for surveillance to monitor trends in HIV infection. This requires high ANC attendance, universal HIV testing for pregnant women, and accurate recording of HIV-positive women, including those already on ART before their first ANC visit. 7. The number and percentage of people living with HIV on ART who initiated tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment (TPT) measures the extent to which ART patients are starting treatment for latent TB infection. TPT is a critical component of preventing TB-related morbidity and mortality among people living with HIV. 8. The number and percentage of people living with HIV on ART who completed a course of TPT among those who initiated it measures the effectiveness of scaled-up TPT programs. This indicator assesses the proportion of patients completing the recommended TPT course, which is essential for the TB/HIV service cascade. 9. The percentage of people living with HIV with TB symptoms who receive a rapid molecular test, such as Xpert MTB/RIF, as a first diagnostic test for TB measures the program's ability to provide recommended diagnostic testing for TB among HIV-positive individuals. 10. The percentage of people living with HIV newly initiated on ART who have active TB disease measures the burden of active TB among this population. Early detection of TB enables prompt treatment and early ART initiation, indirectly reflecting efforts to detect HIV-associated TB. 11. The percentage of people living with HIV newly initiated on ART who were screened for TB symptoms measures the extent to which routine TB screening is conducted among this population. Screening is critical at ART initiation when immune compromise is greatest. 12. The percentage of people living with HIV newly initiated on ART and screened for TB symptoms who screened positive measures the effectiveness of TB screening in identifying presumptive TB cases. Low positivity rates may indicate inadequate or poor-quality screening, particularly in high-burden settings. 13. The percentage of people living with HIV newly initiated on ART and screened positive for TB symptoms who then undergo appropriate TB diagnostic testing measures the program's ability to ensure proper follow-up for individuals with positive TB symptom screening. This indicator highlights obstacles between positive screening and diagnostic testing based on national clinical guidelines.
